title: Feed all 12 chutes of a riffle splitter evenly, tipping a full-width pan of sand with its lip held level by both hands
instruction: Split the sand sample in the pan into two halves with the riffle splitter.
context: Civil engineering technologists and technicians (O*NET 17-3022.00) cut field samples of concrete sand down to test size before a sieve analysis. ASTM C702 has the sample poured from a pan as wide as the row of chutes, spread from edge to edge so that approximately equal amounts flow through each chute (Iowa DOT IM 336 repeats it). The chutes alternate between the two catch pans, so a pour that favors one end of the row or a corner feeds a few chutes and gives halves of different size and gradation, and the tested half no longer represents the stockpile. In practice a loaded pan this wide is held by both ends to keep its lip level, so here each hand takes one end handle and both tip it together over the hopper. Unlike the two-handed pot pour into a bowl (#463), the score is how evenly each of the 12 chutes is fed and how close the split comes to half and half, not whether the sand lands.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Everything is fixed except the pour pan. A bench riffle splitter for fine aggregate stands centered at x 22, y 0: 12 chutes 1.27 cm (1/2 in) wide between 1.6 mm aluminum vanes make a row 17.3 cm long along y; its open hopper mouth, 6 cm across x (x 19 to 25), has its top 10 cm above the table, held by two aluminum end plates (8 cm along x, 10 cm tall) at y +/-8.8, each topped by a 6 mm flange that tips stray sand into the end chute. Each chute's floor slopes down to an outlet 4.5 cm up, the chutes alternating: the first one at the robot's right (-y) empties toward the robot, the next away from it, and so on. Two steel catch pans (5 x 19 cm inside, 3.5 cm walls) sit under the outlets, centered at x 14.8 and x 29.2, y 0. A steel pour pan (300 g, 967 g loaded) sits on the table centered at x 38, y 0: inside 10 cm along x by 17.2 cm along y (2.4 mm narrower than the chute row, as C702 asks), 3 mm floor, 4.5 cm walls on its far side and both ends, and a 6 mm lip along the side facing the splitter (its outer face at x 32.9). Flat steel handle bars 2.5 cm wide and 2 cm tall, 2 to 4 cm above the table, run from each end wall out to y +/-16; a stock pan has short end tabs, and these are lengthened (our invention) so the two grippers can hold them 28 cm apart, at y +/-14. The pan holds 667 g of dry concrete sand (1.45 g/mL loose, 34-degree angle of repose), spread evenly along its width and banked against the far wall: level with the walls' top over the back 2.6 cm, its face sloping at 34 degrees down to the floor 8 mm behind the lip. The sand is drawn tan: as columns in the pan, a stream wherever it pours, one ridge in a catch pan under each chute's outlet (its height shows that chute's grams) and flat piles where it spills.
scoring: The pan is set down when its underside is within 8 mm of the table, it is within 10 degrees of level and still, and every tool point and pad tip is at least 1 cm clear of the pan and its handles (let go). The pour is two-handed when at least 90 % of the grams that went down the chutes ran while each handle bar had its own gripper closed on it (fingers stopped by the 2.5 cm bar, tool point within 1 cm of it). The splitter is fed evenly when every chute carried within 35 % of the mean chute's grams (a lip held more than about 4.5 degrees off level, one end 1.4 cm lower, or about 5 mm off center along the row fails it; sand falling on an end flange counts in the end chute). Scores: 0 if the pan is not set down (including still holding it), if the pour was not two-handed (one hand on a handle or anywhere else on the pan), or if less than half of the sample went down the chutes (doing nothing, pouring onto the table or straight into a catch pan). 1.0 if at least 97 % went down the chutes (at most 20 g left in the pan or lost), at most 2 % (13 g) was spilled or fell past the hopper straight into a catch pan, the splitter was fed evenly, each catch pan holds 45 to 55 % of the sample (300 to 367 g, so each half meets ASTM C136's 300 g minimum for a fine aggregate sieve analysis), and both arms are back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started); 0.9 for the same with an arm not home. 0.5 if at least 90 % went down the chutes, at most 5 % was lost, every chute within 60 % of the mean (the pour reached the whole row, about 4.5 to 7 degrees off level) and each catch pan holds 40 to 60 %. 0.25 otherwise (half or more went down the chutes, but unevenly or with a spill). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, fit each catch pan with five thin dividers so each chute's sand lands in its own compartment, weigh every compartment and the sand left in the pan on a 0.1 g scale, sweep and weigh the table, and check on the video that the pan ends flat on the table, let go.
run_limit: 1,500 steps (75 seconds at 20 Hz; the demo takes 654)
reset_notes: Pour both catch pans and any sand swept from the table back into the pour pan, top it up to 667 g on a scale, spread it evenly along the width and bank it against the far wall, set the pan at its taped spot (lip toward the splitter) and slide the empty catch pans back under the outlets.
fidelity: The sand is a scored bulk model, not particles: each step it stands at its angle of repose in 24 strips across the pan, pours over each strip's lip by a weir law, drifts toward the low end of a pan tipped sideways, and falls plumb into the chute or catch pan below (or onto the table). Chutes never clog, and the sand's 667 g stays in the pan's mass while it pours. The hopper is 10 cm tall (a bench splitter's is about 20 cm) so the arms reach over it.
